extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum-makers, and educated general readers interested in the aims of liberal education and language instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative argument about whether the study of Greek and Latin (the 'classics') is essential to a liberal education, versus prioritizing mastery of the mother-tongue and modern scientific/philosophical studies. The page discusses criteria for what kinds of studies 'educate' (give insight or develop capacity) and recommends curricular priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and refined use of the mother-tongue as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: An accurate and refined use of the mother-tongue is the only mental acquisition that is an essential part of the education of a lady or a gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other subjects (Greek, Latin, modern languages, mathematics, sciences, metaphysics, history, aesthetics) are profitable but not essential; the 'fruit' of liberal education is capacity and desire to learn (power), not mere knowledge. Mastery of the native language is repeatedly foregrounded as the primary aim and foundation of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insight-giving studies must induce cultural self-alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: Insight-giving studies are those that 'lead the individual out of his immediate and familiar surroundings, and cause him to breathe the atmosphere and become familiar with the accessory conditions of an earlier historical stage' of the culture from which he derives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is W. T. Harris's criterion for valuing classics: they effect 'self-alienation' which he argues is necessary to self-knowledge. The essay treats this as a testable claim about what kinds of studies yield insight into institutions and civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between mathematics and classics as sources of insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics, as the science of general relations of time and space, is related to insight into the physical world; Harris argues classics have the same relation to insight into the world of institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author critiques this analogy: if one wants a study of the same formal order as mathematics for insight into institutions, logic (not Latin/Greek) would be appropriate. This is a criterion for testing the kind of study appropriate for institutional insight (formal science vs contingent cultural study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/benefit of 'self-alienation' (learning to think in a dead language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris's claim that learning to 'think in their idioms' (Greek/Latin) captures feelings and phantasies lost in translation implies the price of 'self-alienation' — investing large portions of life to become mentally native to another tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the gains (access to earlier stages of feeling/phantasy) justify the costs (years of study, potential alienation from one's vernacular and arrested development). The author judges the cost typically too high and impractical for all but a vanishingly small minority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mother-tongue as sole medium of mental development
rubrics_metrics.description: We think only in our mother-tongue; it is the sole medium by which our self-activity and mental development are determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, curricular priority should be given to mastering the mother-tongue before foreign or classical languages. Dead languages are characterized as counteractive instruments that can 'shackle the mind' if given precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of language via study of native masterpieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The obvious way to master the mother-tongue is to study it in its own masterpieces (the established practice of the best writers and speakers), rather than by studying foreign tongues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying native masterpieces enriches vocabulary, preserves syntax, and perfects expression without corrupting usage; this method suffices for achieving 'accurate and refined use' of the language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign/dead languages are means of knowledge, not necessary to culture
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of foreign languages (especially dead languages) is a means of acquiring knowledge but is not necessary or convenient as a means of culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may enlarge vocabulary or knowledge incidentally, but can cramp expression and impede mastering one's native syntax. Thus they should not be treated as indispensable in a scheme of general education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize living sciences and philosophy alongside English
rubrics_metrics.description: If reorganizing education, bring mathematics, chemistry, physiology, and (natural, moral, and mental) philosophy to the front, under the immediate command of English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends replacing dead-language centrality with a curriculum emphasizing sciences and philosophy plus mastery of English; glossology (comparative philology) is important but not central to general education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-culture study for English-speakers is English, not Latin/Greek
rubrics_metrics.description: For English-speaking peoples, the 'special-culture study' that best transmits cultural insight is English itself, not Latin or Greek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that the 'tap-root' of mental growth for English-speakers is English; neglecting it dwarfs intellect, while cherishing it yields full intellectual stature. This functions as a standard for curricular selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and gatekeeping role of classics in professions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dead languages have historically been used as gatekeepers to professions, obstructing admission to those unable to meet classic-language requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural critique serves as an evaluative criterion: if a curricular requirement primarily functions to exclude rather than educate, its legitimacy should be questioned. The author treats such gatekeeping as an argument against imposed classical prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical test: cultures mastering their vernaculars produce high intellects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence from literature and other cultures (Shakespeare, Icelandic Njala, Chinese mandarins) shows that exclusive study/mastery of a vernacular can produce outstanding native literary and intellectual achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative/historical examples to evaluate whether classical study is necessary: the success of cultures that emphasize their native tongue contradicts the claim that knowledge of foreign tongues is essential for native mastery or culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between erudition and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Erudition (learning/learning of the past) is not synonymous with education; education is the means to erudition and is essentially mastery of one's own language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum should aim at cultivating faculties and capacity (education) rather than merely accumulating erudition; prioritize methods that grow capacity (language mastery, sciences, reasoning) over accumulation of classical erudition.
